Inside the ring the rock gave off a faint dry ticking he called drauvel, for want of a word, and he could not count it because it would not hold still. The ossling had left no new trail. The hreldane knocked three times and he kept it out of the columns. The vothrimm stayed silent. The skarnel faced south. On the rope, the stranger's knot had moved another place nearer his hand.

text: On the twenty-third day of the lichen count, the fifty-fifth without the mailboat in that year of 1911, Hjalti kept his rope coiled away from the brimnakk, yet at dawn the tjorvask on it read one twelve and eleven, and his thumb could not rub it off. So the wrong-slanted hand counts by days, not by layings. text: Hesper cast the seven stakes as ordered, then an eighth nobody had asked for. Into its bronze she dropped the clapper of a cracked hand-bell from the drowned chapel at Sennet Howe, and she stamped it not 4478 but 4483, skipping five. Wrong on purpose, she wrote on a mould ticket; let the tally stumble. Ilmo stopped humming mid-plum. When the stake had cooled Hesper struck the bronze tongue on the rafter. Seven tones, a pause, then eleven, ragged, as though something counting had lost its place and begun again in a hurry. Mosul, who had stood two days on the threshold, walked in at last and settled on the eighth stake like a hen on an egg. Odalys wrapped it, still warm, in sealskin.

text: Hesper did not point east. She lifted down her mother's order-book, bound in bellows-leather, and thumbed to a page gone brown. Uthwen Skarrow, it read, one peat-spade, the blade to be tuned, not sharpened; paid in forty-one cakes of bog-wax. Underneath, in the mother's hand: she cuts only where the ground hums back, and brings up no fuel. What she brought up, the pedlar Brannoch Ley had sworn at the time, were slabs with footprints pressed in them, a woman's, leading nowhere, stacked like slates behind her hut. Odalys looked at her boots. Ilmo, pale, said the lower dormitory was floored in just such slabs, black and dished, and that the Provost had the boys sleep barefoot. Far up the eastern slope, a ptarmigan called once.

text: The spade had come home long ago. Hesper found it under the quenching trough, where her mother had left it for a repair never collected, swaddled in a pedlar's oilcloth. She did not strike it; she stood it blade-down on the anvil and let go. It hummed by itself, one tone, the tone the bronze tongue had given unstruck. Folded in the oilcloth was Brannoch Ley's bill of sale: to Uthwen Skarrow, thirteen cobbler's lasts in pearwood, cut by Pell Auchterlow, all left feet, all to one measure. Twelve delivered. The thirteenth lay there under the bill, grey with age, its heel worn. Ilmo turned it over. Odalys unlaced her left boot without being asked, and Hesper, watching her hands, put down the chalk.

text: Nobody watched the fitting. They watched the egg, which had turned itself on the bench until its blunt end faced the humming spade. So Hesper read the back of the bill instead. Pell Auchterlow's pencil: measured from no woman, only from a slab she sent, the 23rd of Marth. No right foot was sent. I asked. She said the right one comes down somewhere else. Beneath it, Brannoch Ley's scrawl: Uthwen would not take the twelve after all, so he had sold them on as net-floats to the ferrywoman Maud Isterby at Carrow Wath, who complained ever after that they drifted upstream. Ilmo said, quietly, that every print in the dormitory floor was a left one too. Odalys laced her boot again and said nothing.

text: At dawn the millrace began to click. Ilmo found them first: nine pearwood lasts nosing toes-first against the sluice-grate, still knotted to a torn strip of net. They had come thirty-seven miles up from Carrow Wath against the water, over the weir at Gant Ollery, which nothing climbs. The net held no fish, only Maud Isterby's brass ferry-tally, notched seven, then eleven. Three cords ended in fray; three lasts had not stopped here. Hesper laid the nine on the bench beside the thirteenth and ran her thumb along each heel. She chalked: worn alike, and these were never walked in. The egg, unhurried, turned its blunt end from the spade toward the race. Odalys counted the missing three aloud, twice, as if they might answer.

text: Hesper did not trust her thumb twice. She took down the assay balance her mother had bought from Corvin Thrale and weighed the lasts one by one against the thirteenth. Each of the nine came up light by fifteen grains, no more, no less. She left them standing on a sheet of blacked paper while the furnace was fed; by noon there was a pale crescent of pearwood dust behind every heel, though nobody had touched them. She chalked: not walked in. Walked with. Ilmo, meanwhile, had turned over the brass ferry-tally. On its back a third row had begun, one notch, bright as a new coin. He held it out flat on his palm, and a second thin curl of brass lifted by itself and fell.

text: Odalys swept the nine crescents of pearwood dust into a snuff tin with a ptarmigan feather, because dust was the one thing in the foundry nobody had yet asked a question of. She stretched her survey drumskin over the quenching trough, sifted the dust across it, and stood the tuned spade beside it to hum. The dust did not make the star-figures she knew from the Institute. It crept into rings, one inside another, off-centre, with a dark wedge left bare on the northern side. Hesper counted them by thumb: twenty-seven. She chalked: one tree, felled at twenty-seven, struck by lightning first. Ilmo knew of only one burnt pear orchard, at Lissom Varr, and said the stumps there still flowered. On his palm the tally cut a third notch.

text: Hesper laid her palm flat on the tuned spade and stilled it. The rings of dust did not slump. Instead the drumskin went on sounding with nothing to drive it: one long low roll, slower than any drum, which Odalys knew at once for thunder played back at walking pace. Hesper put her other hand in the quenching trough and counted the tremor through the water, thirty-one heartbeats from first to last. When it ended, a single thread of dust had crossed the bare wedge, running outward from the heart of the stump toward the bark. Hesper chalked: wrong way. Ilmo nodded. The old orchard-keeper at Lissom Varr, Orrin Sabelthwaite, had always told the dormitory boys the same thing: that pear tree was never struck from the sky. The egg rocked once.

text: The trough would not come to rest. Long after the drumskin fell silent the water stood heaped toward its eastern end, a hand's breadth higher there, as if the foundry floor had tipped. Hesper, to test it, drew a stake-blank from the fire and plunged it in. No hiss, no steam; the bronze came out still glowing, and the water was colder than before. Ilmo, hungry again at last, dipped a ladle and drank. Perry, he said, the hard kind, the kind Jessamy Coldwether pressed at Lissom Varr and paid the orchard-keeper in, forty-five flagons a winter, to keep his stories for boys and away from the Provost. Hesper tasted, spat, and chalked: not water now. On the bench the brass tally cut a fourth notch. Mosul's egg had begun to sweat.

text: The stake-blank would not cool. By dusk it lay on the anvil still the colour of a cherry, and Ilmo, dared by nobody, picked it up bare-handed: no warmer than a spoon. It gave light without heat, and the light was particular. Under it Hesper's fresh chalk marks vanished, but old scratches showed. Odalys carried it along the bench like a candle, and beneath the pan of the assay balance, where daylight had shown plain brass, a stamp stood up: Corvin Thrale, maker, and under his name, true for weights that have walked, proved at Wenhollow Scar, 51 paces. Not grains. Paces. Hesper read it twice by thumb and chalked nothing. The sweat on Mosul's egg had beaded, and every bead leaned toward the glow.

text: Odalys lifted the cold glow toward the rafter. The bronze tongue, poured by Hesper only days before, ought to have gone blank under that light, the way the chalk did. It did not. Along its edge stood a founder's mark, worn soft as an old coin: Idony Dunmarrow, pour 63. Hesper's mother, long dead, whose order-book stopped at sixty-two. Hesper climbed the stool and read it by thumb, then held her own palms under the glow as if they might be signed too. They were only scarred. On the floor Odalys's sooty bootprints had vanished entirely, and the boy's with them. One track stayed: bare, left-footed, crossing from the door to the trough. Ilmo set his foot beside it and took it back. Mosul's egg ticked.

text: Maud Isterby came at dusk, on foot, thirty-seven miles of towpath in her knees, and did not look at the cold glow or the bare track. She wanted her net. Hesper gave her the torn strip; Ilmo held out the brass tally, and Maud put her hands behind her back. Not that, she said. For 33 nights a fare had stood on Dunnock Stair, the far landing at Carrow Wath, ringing no bell, asking to be taken not across but along. She had refused each time. A ferry goes from bank to bank; she would carry nothing lengthwise up a river. She had notched each refusal out of habit. Then the tally began notching without her. In Ilmo's palm it cut a fifth. The egg's ticking stopped to listen.

text: Hesper chalked: what did it offer. Maud snorted. Nothing a body could spend. Each morning after a refusal she found one knot tied in her mooring rope, a knot she had never learned and could not pick loose, the kind only old Tamsin Arkwold the rope-walker used, and Tamsin was 57 years in the ground. Maud had cut out thirty-two and thrown them to the current. The thirty-third she kept. She drew it from her apron: a fist of hemp, still dripping, though she had walked two days dry. Since she pocketed it, she said, her boat the Patient Wren lies bow-upstream at its mooring, straining against the river like a dog at a door. Odalys reached for the knot. It tightened.

text: Oelrich said the dead weaver was Perpetua Stahl, a ropewalker's widow who had lost her right arm to a capstan and ordered everything turned about. She died in January with the loom unpaid. Ilmari stood before it a long while. Then he remembered his sister Sanna at school, caned across the knuckles for writing with the wrong hand, and he counted out the money. In the loom still lay Perpetua's shuttle, carved from a swan's breastbone, with a child's milk tooth rattling inside. Oelrich would not say whose. In the Fischergrube cellar Thorn unpicked his oilskin and laid down eleven watch movements, one by one, without whistling. Brodersen turned the first escapement over, breathed on it, and began. The goat watched.

Ilmari looked at the half-built clock, whose single hand had begun, haltingly, to creep backwards. The goat went on chewing.

text: On Thursday the Vasa steamer came up the Trave in a brown rain. Evert Nylund walked down the gangway last, a tall man in a beaver collar, carrying the hatbox in both arms like an infant. Wendt was waiting. The narwhal tusk tapped the lid once and gave back the wrong sound. "Granite," he said in Swedish, "undeclared mineral, eleven kilos," and wrote out a receipt in violet ink. Evert did not argue; he counted the buttons on Wendt's coat aloud, as he counted everything. Ilmari, behind a salt cart, set the spare blue eye on a bollard, gazing downriver toward the sea. Evert saw it, stopped counting at seven, and followed its stare the wrong way along the quay.

text: Stoneless, Evert Nylund counted Lübeck: forty-one steps at the Marienkirche, seven gables in the Glockengiesserstrasse, six crate-nails in Oelrich's mouth. The loom stood half boxed, addressed to Sanna Kvist. Oelrich lifted the swan-bone shuttle to wrap it, and it rattled. Evert stopped at six. From his waistcoat he took a snuff tin and shook it against his ear: the same dry note, many times over. "Nineteen," he said. "I have had nineteen since I was seven. Perpetua Stahl was our nursemaid in Vasa. She pulled the twentieth with a thread and a door and told me the mice took it." He held out his hand, quite steady. Oelrich put the shuttle behind his back. Ilmari, in the doorway, stopped breathing.

text: Ilmari breathed. "Twenty for one," he said. "Your tooth, and you drown nobody." Evert opened his shirt. Round his waist, wound three times, ran a tarred cord. "Four hundred knots. One for each mark. That is a count too." Oelrich, sighing, tilted the shuttle; the tooth would not pass the thread-hole until he drew it through on a loop of waxed linen, small and brown as a barley grain. It dropped into the tin. Evert shook it, listened, and his shoulders came down an inch. Ilmari laid the change from the loom on the crate: two hundred and twelve marks. Evert untied two hundred and twelve knots aloud, without one mistake. "One hundred and eighty-eight," he said. "Until then he only floats."

text: The cellar off the Fischergrube smelled of solder and goat. Evert ducked under the lintel and the goat, disliking beaver, tore a strip from his collar and stood chewing it. Brodersen did not rise. Beside him the clock breathed: no weight fell in it; a wet sea-sponge on a chain dried, lightened, and rose, and the single hand crept the wrong way round. "I have come to count you," Evert said. "One true eye. One glass. Ten fingers, silvered." Then he looked at the hand, and the numbers turned in his mouth. "Nine. Eight. Seven." He sat down hard on a crate. "Four. Three." Brodersen coughed into his sleeve. "Two more days," he said, "and the inspector shall pay for your knots."

"No," she said to Ilmari. "No," to his cap, his greeting, the daylight. Then the goat walked in, bell knocking, laid its chin on the rim of the tub and licked the ice. She looked at it a long while. His mother stroked the goat's ear. "He was skating," she told it. "Tell him the ice is still good."

text: Saturday, the cellar off the Fischergrube. Without the goat there was no milk, and Brodersen's silvered fingers shook too badly to file the last pallet. He pulled off his wedding ring instead, had Ilmari clamp it in the vice, and talked him through sawing it in half. "Gold forgives," he said. One half went into the escapement and the other into his waistcoat, for Hedda. But the hand stuttered and would not keep time. Then Evert, on his crate, began helplessly to count: "Sixty. Fifty-nine. Fifty-eight." Brodersen lifted his head. "Slower," he said. "Again." All day the man who had brought a stone to drown him called the beats, and the clockmaker bent the hairspring to that voice. At midnight the sponge rose, and the hand crept backwards, steady as breath.

text: Sunday, first light. Ilmari dipped the sponge in a bucket of Trave water and they set out: the clock upright on a fish-barrow, Brodersen folded beside it under a herring sack, Thorn pushing, Evert walking behind calling "Nine. Eight. Seven" to the gulls. Up the third stair in the Engelsgrube the old woman sat with her feet in the ice and the goat against her knee. Wendt held his tusk like a candle. They stood the clock on her windowsill. It ticked. She opened her mouth and did not scream. She watched the hand go back a long while. "Leberecht," she said. "Nine years old, on the Wakenitz, a quarter past three." She reached into the tub and lifted out, frozen in its own block, a red wool mitten. "He will want this."

Round 2 done: at sea, hove-to off the Kvarken skerries, two days out; hold count is 41 against the chalked 43; mate now named Rasmus Thorn, whistles a hymn backwards when pleased. Odd detail R2: blue glass eye wrapped in a page of a Danish almanac for 1897, found between barrels, now in Ilmari's cap with the letter. Round 3 done: third night, middle watch; unlit pilot-gig from the skerries rowed by a woman in a sealskin hood; false bulkhead forward in the hold; the 2 missing barrels are sawn open as berths behind it; in one sits an old one-eyed Dane who asks for his eye back. Odd detail R3: white goat with a brass bell stuffed with moss, handed up from the gig, carried below by Thorn. Round 4 done: still the third night, behind the bulkhead. Dane named Aksel Brodersen, clockmaker of Vasa, owes 400 marks to a brother-in-law who swore to drown him. Goat is there for its milk: his stomach is ruined by mercury from gilding clock dials. Thorn is paid in watch movements, 11 so far, sewn into his oilskin lining. Bargain struck: Ilmari's silence to Lübeck for the price of a loom. Odd detail R4: brass key shaped like a herring, given by Brodersen in place of money, 'it opens what pays'; what it opens is unknown so far. Round 5 done: fifth night, Gotland gale; goat loose on deck, moss shaken out of the bell so it now rings; Ilmari dropped the glass eye and THE GOAT ATE IT (eye is now inside the goat, not returned, not overboard); Thorn did not whistle. The second sawn barrel-berth sprang open: it was meant for Brodersen's wife, the woman in the sealskin hood, who rowed back instead of coming. Odd detail R5: inside that berth, a never-worn yellow silk wedding dress folded round a pair of bone skates. Round 6 done: seventh day, alongside at Travemünde; Zollinspektor Wendt counted 41 against 43 and stopped at the false bulkhead; the goat's bell rang once; Thorn covered it by dropping a marlinspike and swearing; Wendt moved on, bulkhead NOT opened. The herring key fits a hidden drawer under the binnacle: nine empty gold watch-cases, worth two looms (not yet sold). Wife is Hedda; the drowning brother-in-law is HER brother; she rowed back to wind the sixty clocks in the Vasa shop so he hears ticking and thinks Aksel is home. Odd detail R6: Wendt's cane is a narwhal tusk, he taps every plank with it. Lübeck is one tide up the Trave. Round 7 done: Lübeck quay under the salt warehouses, evening tide. Brodersen went ashore inside barrel forty-two with a false head; the goat walked down the plank under the yellow silk dress. Nine watch-cases SOLD to goldsmith Tobias Quandt in the Hüxstrasse; loom money now in hand (two looms' worth, less his cut). The goat passed the blue eye; Brodersen rinsed it in schnapps and wears it again, facing slightly left. Letter to the sister WRITTEN ('The loom is paid for. Ask me nothing about the goat.') but not yet posted. Wendt's tusk heard tapping on the quay behind Ilmari. Odd detail R7: Quandt weighs gold against dried peas, not brass weights. Round 8 done: Quandt's back room in the Hüxstrasse: 312 jars of dried peas, one labelled for each year ('brass can be filed; a pea only shrinks, and shrinks honestly'). Quandt has weighed Brodersen's gilding for twenty years and knows from the peas he is dying of the mercury. Letter to the sister POSTED at the post office in the Königstrasse; Wendt's tusk came down across the slot one moment too late. Wendt now face to face with Ilmari, speaks Swedish, asked 'what is a goat?' (he read or guessed the letter). Odd detail R8: in the pea jar for 1897 lay a SECOND blue glass eye, Brodersen's uncollected spare; it is now in Ilmari's cap. Round 9 done: Ilmari answered that a goat is 'a kind of sheep that gives opinions'. Wendt wants NO duty: he will forget the 41 barrels and the bell in exchange for a clock that runs BACKWARDS. Brodersen is hiding in a cellar off the Fischergrube and says he can build it in a week 'if the mercury allows'. Loom-maker found: Barnabas Oelrich, Glockengiesserstrasse. The loom is beautiful, cheap and ready, but built mirror-wise, LEFT-HANDED throughout, for a weaver who died before collecting it; NOT yet bought. Odd detail R9: Wendt's mother in the Engelsgrube has refused every day since 14 March 1870, and forward-running clocks make her scream. text: At a quarter past three by the backward hand the old woman stood up out of the tub. Water ran from her ankles; forty-one years ran with it. "His skates," she said. Ilmari looked at Thorn, and Thorn, whistling nothing, went down the three stairs and came back with the yellow silk bundle from the cellar. The bone skates lay in her palms, small as herrings. "Shin of an ox," she said. "I greased them myself." Wendt unscrewed the silver ferrule of his narwhal tusk and poured out coins, a long cold stream of them, onto the floorboards. Evert knelt, the tarred cord in his lap, and began to untie. "One hundred and eighty-eight. One hundred and eighty-seven." The goat watched each knot go. Brodersen, against the wall, had not yet drunk.

text: "Two. One." The last knot gave, and the cord lay across Evert's knees, a plain rope. He looked at it a long while. "One," he said again, and then, astonished, "two." The old woman had unbuckled the goat's brass bell, turned it mouth upward, and milked into it, barefoot on the boards. She carried it to the wall herself. Brodersen drank; the grey went a little out of him. "I was nineteen, a journeyman here," he said. "On the Wakenitz that afternoon, carrying a clock to Marli. I heard a cry and set the clock down gently first. When I reached the hole there were only the skates, standing upright in the slush." His glass eye faced left. "I have wound sixty clocks since. None forgave me."

text: A day north over chalk rubble stood the heronry of Whenorra Quysst: forty-four driftwood posts, each topped with a nest coiled from old sounding cord. One heron lived there, footless, propped on two tin stilts, its left socket empty. The nest-warden, Hessaly Quornet, had eggshells stitched to her sleeves; she took the lantern's wire frame as fee and bent it into a cage for a single grey egg. Agnes lowered her one-knot cord down the hollow seventy-first post, though she had counted only forty-four. It came up knotless, limp, wet with brine warm as blood, and tied at its end was a blue glass eye. It fitted the token's hole. Blown two days north, Quornet said, at the glass-pit of Orthwen Tesquilla, where a knotless cord begins counting the other way.

At the top Wrothel Quessary bit her limpet shell and hung it on a nail among nine hundred others, then blew out her eel-oil lantern. She walked the slag ridge north to the bone-kiln of Sarchelyn Ouro, a chimney of stacked whale vertebrae smoking ochre. The raker Ulwith Orrequal refused to light her wick without a shell, took the lantern's glass as payment and ground it into the lime. He showed her the heron foot pressed backward in the ash, heel first, and said the forgery was fired at the kiln before berth 4471 had a number. She climbed the second ladder, quillwort rope with a hundred and four knots, counted with her teeth, to the tally-house of Thessoch Lyre: a shed roofed with coracle hides, sounding cords on pegs, each sealed in lead with the backward heron foot. Yessaril Whorne, who wears a collar of fishing weights, weighed the lantern and took the wick in exchange for a seven-knot cord. She followed lead plugs hammered into the slag north to the sounding-well of Tolliquesh Arn: a barrel-wide shaft kerbed with walrus teeth, windlass a narwhal tusk. Quorrel Hystane, the well-wright with ochre-dyed thumbs, took the lantern's tin handle as fee and bent it into a hook. The seven-knot cord came up with four knots, hot and tasting of rust, and on the hook hung a clay token stamped with a heron that has no feet at all. She crossed the lichen flats, a day north, to the tar-gate of Senwyth Ocalle: two upright whale jaws lashed with quillwort, a curtain of dripping pitch between them. Lowreth Scainquil, the dauber in gull-skin mittens, took the lantern's tin base as fee and hammered it into a ladle, then pressed the clay token into warm tar; it came away with two feet, toes pointing up. The four-knot cord, lowered through a knothole in the sill, came up with two knots, sticky and smelling of burnt hair. Half a day north over shingle that rings like crockery she reached the stamp-loft of Yoncherel Atwhiss: a loft on six stilts of sperm-whale rib, climbed by a quillwort net, floor strewn with brass filings and cuttlebone. Chesswyn Tarloquil, the die-cutter with a thimble on every finger, took the lantern's tin hood as fee and snipped it into eleven blank discs. The token's tar feet matched the old die, but the die's heron has no eye, only a drilled hole. The two-knot cord, lowered through that hole, came up with one knot, frozen stiff and tasting of chalk. Tarloquil said the die was only copied; the bird itself was drawn from life at the heronry of Whenorra Quysst. A day north over chalk rubble she reached the heronry: forty-four driftwood posts, each topped with a nest coiled from old sounding cord, and one living heron, footless, propped on two tin stilts, its left socket empty. Hessaly Quornet, the nest-warden with eggshells stitched to her sleeves, took the lantern's wire frame as fee and bent it into a cage for a single grey egg. The one-knot cord, lowered down the hollow seventy-first post (she counted twice; there are only forty-four), came up with no knots, limp, wet with brine warm as blood, and tied at its end was a blue glass eye. Pressed into the token, the eye fits the hole. Quornet said the eye was blown two days north at the glass-pit of Orthwen Tesquilla, and that a knotless cord starts counting the other way. Two days north, chalk giving way to black sand, she reached the glass-pit: a crater floored with fused green slag, ringed by forty-four blowpipes of hollow heron leg-bone. Wynchorel Usqueth, the blower with white-scarred lips and an apron of sewn fish-bladders, took the top horn button of her coat as fee (the coat had nine; eight remain) and melted it into a bead. He said the blue eye is one of a pair and the other was never blown for a bird. The knotless cord, lowered into the cooling-well, came up with one knot, slick and grey, tied by a hagfish below. Three days north, black sand ending in frost-heaved mud, she reached the hag-weir of Quornessa Ythril: seventy-one wicker pens staked across a brackish creek, each roofed with a walrus scapula. Tesswyn Orquilleth, the weir-keeper in clogs of whale-ear bone who keeps her slime in corked gourds, took the second horn button as fee (seven remain) and sewed it over the blind eye-spot of a breeding hagfish, as a lid. The one-knot cord, fed into the deepest pen, came up with two knots, cold and ropy with slime, and looped through them a lead plaque showing the heron face-on, with two eyes. Orquilleth said the second blue eye was bartered four days north to the salt-loom of Hyrcquess Olwenta, and woven in. Four days north, mud stiffening to grey salt-pan, she reached the salt-loom: a frame of two sperm-whale jaws wide as a barn door, warped with hagfish-slime thread drawn through brine until it crusts white, hung with seventy-one loom-weights. Orchessly Quenwith, the weaver with a salt-cracked tongue and a necklace of loom-weights, took the third horn button as fee (six remain) and hung it on the warp as a seventy-second weight. On the loom hangs a heron's hood of salt-cloth, made face-on (hence the plaque), the second blue eye woven into its right socket, the left socket open. The two-knot cord, sunk in the brine vat, came up with three knots, crusted and tasting of iron, and tied to it a whalebone needle threaded with hair of Agnes's own colour. Quenwith said the hood was ordered from five days north, from the ice-press of Thyssequorn Awle. Five days north, salt-pan cracking into shore-ice, she reached the ice-press: two walrus-hide platens the size of doors, screwed together by a narwhal tusk turned with a capstan of ribs; it presses the brine out of sea-ice until the panes come clear as spectacles. Lorquesswyn Athrel, the presser in slit-whalebone snow-goggles who breathes through a sponge, took the fourth horn button as fee (five remain) and fitted it as a washer under the tusk. In the order-rack stands a pane holding the print of a face, face-on, left eye shut: Agnes's own, pressed before she arrived; the hood was measured from it. The three-knot cord, fed down the drain-hole, came up with four knots, rimed and tasting of lamp-smoke, and tied to it a tin disc stamped 4472 (one of the eleven blanks snipped from her lantern hood). Athrel said the pane was sent from six days north, from the lamp-grave of Yrchwessel Quoth. Six days north, shore-ice thickening to blue shelf, she reached the lamp-grave: seventy-one lanterns buried upright in the ice, only their tin chimneys showing, each capped with a limpet shell. Quessoril Thawny, the wick-sexton in a coat of stitched lamp-wicks who carries a snuffer made from a heron's skull, took the fifth horn button as fee (four remain) and laid it as a lid on the seventy-second chimney. Under that chimney burns Agnes's own lantern, reassembled: glass, wick, handle, base, wire frame, hood with eleven holes, lit before she came. The four-knot cord, lowered down the chimney, came up with five knots, sooty and tasting of horn, and tied to it a limpet shell bearing her own bite (the one Quessary hung on the nail). Thawny said the pane was pressed by a woman with one eye shut who came down from seven days north, from the button-quay of Welchyssa Orth. Seven days north, blue shelf fraying into pack-ice, she reached the button-quay: a jetty of seventy-one floes sewn edge to edge with hair rope, every stitch fastened by a horn button, five of them Agnes's own spent ones, already worn smooth. Yllthwessa Quorne, the button-reeve with thread-grooves in her gums who bites her knots shut, took the sixth horn button as fee (three remain) and, borrowing the whalebone needle and using up its hair thread, sewed the button to a seventy-second floe as a cleat stamped 4472. The five-knot cord, fed through that buttonhole, came up with six knots, waxed and tasting of wet wool, and tied to it a strip of coat-front with nine empty buttonholes. Quorne said the shut-eyed woman walked off the quay eight days north, to the hair-ropewalk of Thessquorly Wenth, where the quay's rope is twisted. Eight days north, pack-ice locking into one grey sheet, she reached the hair-ropewalk: an ice-trench seventy-one paces long, roofed with stretched seal-gut, one rope of hair of Agnes's own colour running its length over forked gull-bones. Hwessoril Quarnthey, the ropewalker who walks backward in boots soled with combs and keeps a hank wound round her waist, took the seventh horn button as fee (two remain), filed three grooves in it and used it as the top that lays the strands. The six-knot cord, fed into the hank-hole at the seventy-second pace, came up with seven knots, greasy and tasting of tallow, and tied to it a plait of hair of her own colour, still warm at the cut end. Quarnthey said the hair is combed out nine days north, at the comb-midden of Athwyrquess Olne. Nine days north, the grey sheet buckling into pressure ridges, she reached the comb-midden: a heap of seventy-one broken combs of horn and baleen, tall as a boat shed, combings blowing off it like smoke. Quethorsyl Wharne, the comber with baleen fingernails who stores nits in a walrus bladder, took the eighth horn button as fee (one remains), sawed nine teeth into its rim and tossed it on the heap as the seventy-second comb. The seven-knot cord, pushed down the louse-hole at the heap's core, came up with eight knots, dry and tasting of scalp, and tied to it a baleen comb with one tooth left, a single hair in it wet at the root. Agnes threaded the bare needle with a hair from the plait and sewed the strip of nine empty buttonholes onto her own coat-front. Wharne said the hair is shorn ten days north, at the shearing-stool of Syllquornet Hathwe. Ten days north, the pressure ridges flattening into wind-polished blue ice, she reached the shearing-stool: seventy-one whale-ear bones stacked knee-high, beside shears made of two walrus tusks. Thessaquyn Worlech, the shearer in a wig of gull-down who keeps her whetstone under her tongue, took the ninth and last horn button as fee (none remain) and wedged it under the stool as the seventy-second bone. Then she sat Agnes down and shore her to the scalp; the hair fell already plaited (so the hair was hers all along). The eight-knot cord, dropped down the clip-hole beneath the stool, came up with nine knots, bristly and tasting of whetstone, and tied to it a salt-cloth eyelid stitched shut with hair. Worlech said the lid is sewn eleven days north, at the lid-bench of Orquesswyth Hanle, where buttons are not taken. Eleven days north, the blue ice dulling under blown salt, she reached the lid-bench: seventy-one walrus scapulae laid end to end, salt-cloth eyelids pegged along them to dry like fish skins. Wessaquorn Thyrle, the lid-sewer with lashes of hagfish thread who wears a limpet-shell thimble on every finger and one bare thumb, took Agnes's bitten limpet shell as fee and wore it on the bare thumb. Then she threaded the whalebone needle with the wet-rooted hair from the comb and sewed the salt-cloth lid over Agnes's left eye (so Agnes is now the shut-eyed woman). The nine-knot cord, lowered through the peg-hole of a seventy-second scapula, came up with ten knots, damp and tasting of tears, and tied to it a corked phial of heron leg-bone, warm, with something sloshing in it. Thyrle said tears are boiled off twelve days north, at the tear-still of Hylquessorn Wathe. Decisions made: fees were paid in the coat's horn buttons, one per stop, each put to some odd use by the taker; the buttons are all spent, so fees now come out of the things the cord has brought up (the limpet shell went first, as a thimble); the knots are tied by hagfish, one more each stop; the days north grow by one each stop (next is twelve). Tessaly is a depth, not a name: forty-four then seventy-one knots at the raft, nineteen at Ormsk Vethi, eleven and warm at the kiln, seven, cold and dry at the tally-house, four, hot and rusty at the well, two, sticky and smelling of burnt hair at the tar-gate, one, frozen and tasting of chalk at the stamp-loft, none, warm and briny at the heronry, one again, slick and grey, at the glass-pit, two, cold and ropy with slime, at the hag-weir, three, salt-crusted and tasting of iron, at the salt-loom, four, rimed and tasting of lamp-smoke, at the ice-press, five, sooty and tasting of horn, at the lamp-grave, six, waxed and tasting of wet wool, at the button-quay, seven, greasy and tasting of tallow, at the ropewalk, eight, dry and tasting of scalp, at the comb-midden, nine, bristly and tasting of whetstone, at the shearing-stool, ten, damp and tasting of tears, at the lid-bench. Idris Pallwick's seal is said to be a forgery older than the lighthouse; the feet were added later, and the eye was never cut, it was blown in glass, one of a pair; the second eye is woven into the right socket of a salt-cloth heron hood, which is too large for any bird because it was measured from an ice pane bearing the print of Agnes's own face with the left eye shut; that pane came from the lamp-grave, where it was pressed by a one-eyed-shut woman from the north, whose coat-front (nine buttonholes, all empty) came up on the cord at the button-quay, and whose hair (Agnes's colour, in fact Agnes's own, shorn at the stool) is twisted into the quay's rope at the ropewalk and combed at the midden; everything taken from Agnes going north is turning up ahead of her, already used; the 72nd of everything (weight, chimney, floe, pace, comb, ear bone, scapula) is hers, and the 72nd floe is berth 4472; with her left eye sewn under the salt-cloth lid Agnes now matches the pane, so the shut-eyed woman who came south to press it is most likely Agnes herself, later. Next step: twelve days north to the tear-still of Hylquessorn Wathe. Agnes now has no lantern (it burns in the grave), no limpet shell (it is Thyrle's thumb thimble), a shorn scalp, her left eye sewn shut under a salt-cloth lid, a coat with no buttons and the strip of nine empty buttonholes sewn onto its front, a ten-knot cord (gaining), a clay token whose heron has tar feet with toes pointing up and a blue glass eye, a lead plaque of the heron face-on with two eyes, a whalebone needle (bare again), a tin disc stamped 4472, a warm plait of hair of her own colour (one hair shorter), a baleen comb with one tooth left (its hair used for the lid), and a corked heron-leg-bone phial, warm and sloshing. The lid-sewer, Wessaquorn Thyrle, who has lashes of hagfish thread and wears a limpet-shell thimble on every finger and one bare thumb, took Agnes's bitten limpet shell as fee and wore it on the thumb. Then she threaded the whalebone needle with the wet-rooted hair from the comb and sewed the salt-cloth lid over Agnes's left eye. The nine-knot cord, lowered through the peg-hole of a seventy-second scapula, came up with ten knots, damp and tasting of tears, and tied to it a corked phial of heron leg-bone, warm and sloshing. Tears, Thyrle said, are boiled off twelve days north, at the tear-still of Hylquessorn Wathe.

Quessoril Thawny, the wick-sexton in a coat of stitched lamp-wicks who carries a snuffer made from a heron's skull, took the fifth horn button as fee (four remain) and laid it as a lid on the seventy-second chimney. Under that chimney burns Agnes's own lantern, reassembled: glass, wick, handle, base, wire frame, hood with eleven holes, lit before she came. The four-knot cord, lowered down the chimney, came up with five knots, sooty and tasting of horn, and tied to it a limpet shell bearing her own bite (the one Quessary hung on the nail). Thawny said the pane was pressed by a woman with one eye shut who came down from seven days north, from the button-quay of Welchyssa Orth. Seven days north, blue shelf fraying into pack-ice, she reached the button-quay: a jetty of seventy-one floes sewn edge to edge with hair rope, every stitch fastened by a horn button, five of them Agnes's own spent ones, already worn smooth. Yllthwessa Quorne, the button-reeve with thread-grooves in her gums who bites her knots shut, took the sixth horn button as fee (three remain) and, borrowing the whalebone needle and using up its hair thread, sewed the button to a seventy-second floe as a cleat stamped 4472. The five-knot cord, fed through that buttonhole, came up with six knots, waxed and tasting of wet wool, and tied to it a strip of coat-front with nine empty buttonholes. Quorne said the shut-eyed woman walked off the quay eight days north, to the hair-ropewalk of Thessquorly Wenth, where the quay's rope is twisted. Eight days north, pack-ice locking into one grey sheet, she reached the hair-ropewalk: an ice-trench seventy-one paces long, roofed with stretched seal-gut, one rope of hair of Agnes's own colour running its length over forked gull-bones. Hwessoril Quarnthey, the ropewalker who walks backward in boots soled with combs and keeps a hank wound round her waist, took the seventh horn button as fee (two remain), filed three grooves in it and used it as the top that lays the strands. The six-knot cord, fed into the hank-hole at the seventy-second pace, came up with seven knots, greasy and tasting of tallow, and tied to it a plait of hair of her own colour, still warm at the cut end. Quarnthey said the hair is combed out nine days north, at the comb-midden of Athwyrquess Olne. Nine days north, the grey sheet buckling into pressure ridges, she reached the comb-midden: a heap of seventy-one broken combs of horn and baleen, tall as a boat shed, combings blowing off it like smoke. Quethorsyl Wharne, the comber with baleen fingernails who stores nits in a walrus bladder, took the eighth horn button as fee (one remains), sawed nine teeth into its rim and tossed it on the heap as the seventy-second comb. The seven-knot cord, pushed down the louse-hole at the heap's core, came up with eight knots, dry and tasting of scalp, and tied to it a baleen comb with one tooth left, a single hair in it wet at the root. Agnes threaded the bare needle with a hair from the plait and sewed the strip of nine empty buttonholes onto her own coat-front. Wharne said the hair is shorn ten days north, at the shearing-stool of Syllquornet Hathwe. Ten days north, the pressure ridges flattening into wind-polished blue ice, she reached the shearing-stool: seventy-one whale-ear bones stacked knee-high, beside shears made of two walrus tusks. Thessaquyn Worlech, the shearer in a wig of gull-down who keeps her whetstone under her tongue, took the ninth and last horn button as fee (none remain) and wedged it under the stool as the seventy-second bone. Then she sat Agnes down and shore her to the scalp; the hair fell already plaited (so the hair was hers all along). The eight-knot cord, dropped down the clip-hole beneath the stool, came up with nine knots, bristly and tasting of whetstone, and tied to it a salt-cloth eyelid stitched shut with hair. Worlech said the lid is sewn eleven days north, at the lid-bench of Orquesswyth Hanle, where buttons are not taken. Eleven days north, the blue ice dulling under blown salt, she reached the lid-bench: seventy-one walrus scapulae laid end to end, salt-cloth eyelids pegged along them to dry like fish skins. Wessaquorn Thyrle, the lid-sewer with lashes of hagfish thread who wears a limpet-shell thimble on every finger and one bare thumb, took Agnes's bitten limpet shell as fee and wore it on the bare thumb. Then she threaded the whalebone needle with the wet-rooted hair from the comb and sewed the salt-cloth lid over Agnes's left eye (so Agnes is now the shut-eyed woman). The nine-knot cord, lowered through the peg-hole of a seventy-second scapula, came up with ten knots, damp and tasting of tears, and tied to it a corked phial of heron leg-bone, warm, with something sloshing in it. Thyrle said tears are boiled off twelve days north, at the tear-still of Hylquessorn Wathe. Decisions made: fees were paid in the coat's horn buttons, one per stop, each put to some odd use by the taker; the buttons are all spent, so fees now come out of the things the cord has brought up (the limpet shell went first, as a thimble); the knots are tied by hagfish, one more each stop; the days north grow by one each stop (next is twelve). Tessaly is a depth, not a name: forty-four then seventy-one knots at the raft, nineteen at Ormsk Vethi, eleven and warm at the kiln, seven, cold and dry at the tally-house, four, hot and rusty at the well, two, sticky and smelling of burnt hair at the tar-gate, one, frozen and tasting of chalk at the stamp-loft, none, warm and briny at the heronry, one again, slick and grey, at the glass-pit, two, cold and ropy with slime, at the hag-weir, three, salt-crusted and tasting of iron, at the salt-loom, four, rimed and tasting of lamp-smoke, at the ice-press, five, sooty and tasting of horn, at the lamp-grave, six, waxed and tasting of wet wool, at the button-quay, seven, greasy and tasting of tallow, at the ropewalk, eight, dry and tasting of scalp, at the comb-midden, nine, bristly and tasting of whetstone, at the shearing-stool, ten, damp and tasting of tears, at the lid-bench. Idris Pallwick's seal is said to be a forgery older than the lighthouse; the feet were added later, and the eye was never cut, it was blown in glass, one of a pair; the second eye is woven into the right socket of a salt-cloth heron hood, which is too large for any bird because it was measured from an ice pane bearing the print of Agnes's own face with the left eye shut; that pane came from the lamp-grave, where it was pressed by a one-eyed-shut woman from the north, whose coat-front (nine buttonholes, all empty) came up on the cord at the button-quay, and whose hair (Agnes's colour, in fact Agnes's own, shorn at the stool) is twisted into the quay's rope at the ropewalk and combed at the midden; everything taken from Agnes going north is turning up ahead of her, already used; the 72nd of everything (weight, chimney, floe, pace, comb, ear bone, scapula) is hers, and the 72nd floe is berth 4472; with her left eye sewn under the salt-cloth lid Agnes now matches the pane, so the shut-eyed woman who came south to press it is most likely Agnes herself, later. Next step: twelve days north to the tear-still of Hylquessorn Wathe. Agnes now has no lantern (it burns in the grave), no limpet shell (it is Thyrle's thumb thimble), a shorn scalp, her left eye sewn shut under a salt-cloth lid, a coat with no buttons and the strip of nine empty buttonholes sewn onto its front, a ten-knot cord (gaining), a clay token whose heron has tar feet with toes pointing up and a blue glass eye, a lead plaque of the heron face-on with two eyes, a whalebone needle (bare again), a tin disc stamped 4472, a warm plait of hair of her own colour (one hair shorter), a baleen comb with one tooth left (its hair used for the lid), and a corked heron-leg-bone phial, warm and sloshing. Open questions to advance: what the tear-still is (suggest a retort made of a whale's eardrum-bulla or a row of seventy-one glass alembics blown at the glass-pit, heated over lamp-wick stoves, dripping into limpet shells, the salt scraped off and sent south to the salt-loom); who the still-keeper is (invent a new name) and what she takes as fee (the comb, the plait, the tin disc 4472 or the lead plaque, put to an odd use); what is in the phial (tears from her sewn eye, shed before it was sewn) and what the seventy-second alembic distils from it; what the cord brings up with its eleventh knot; whether the token's blue eye belongs in the hood's open left socket or under her salt-cloth lid; whether a stop soon, thirteen days north or after, is berth 4472 or its far twin, and whether Agnes must then turn south to press the pane. Increase the round number here each time.
